entities.summary:
Antinous Farnese, a marble sculpture created around AD 200, represents the idealized form of Antinous, a young Greek boy who was the beloved companion of Roman Emperor Hadrian. The sculpture, discovered in the 16th century in Rome, serves as a vital artistic representation of the cultural interplay between Hellenistic and Roman ideals of beauty, illustrating the deep emotional connections that were often celebrated in ancient art. The work not only exemplifies the high artistic standards of the Roman Empire but also highlights the significance of personal relationships in Roman society, particularly through the lens of Hadrian’s affection for Antinous, who was deified after his untimely death.

The statue captures the essence of the period's artistry, showcasing the technical prowess of Roman sculptors who could imbue marble with lifelike quality and emotional depth. This particular sculpture is steeped in the narrative of Hadrian’s grief following Antinous's death during a journey to Egypt around AD 130. As a result, Hadrian established a city named Antinopolis in his honor, which further cemented the youth's legacy within the annals of Roman history. The Farnese variant of the sculpture, now housed in the Museo Archeologico Nazionale in Naples, is one of the most celebrated renditions of this theme, influencing later Renaissance artists and their interpretations of beauty and love.
